newsitem.title: FRANCE: French paedophilia probe going overboard -minister.
newsitem.headline: French paedophilia probe going overboard -minister.

text.p: French Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou questioned on Monday whether police and the French media had gone overboard in a mass crackdown on paedophilia, following the suicide of four suspects.
Paedophilia is "abominable...and the pursuit of suspects must be carried out without delay and without hesitation," she said.
"Yet, I wonder whether we need these spectacular arrests and all this media attention," Guigou told Europe 1 radio.
A total of 323 people have been placed under investigation and 24 remanded in custody to date in the nationwide police operation carried out by 2,500 officers.
Among those involved in the round-up have been teachers and clergymen.
The highly-publicised raids initially targeted some 800 individuals whose names were found on a computerised mailing list of a firm selling pornographic video cassettes involving under-age boys.

One of the suspects told France Inter radio he had appeared on the mailing list after contacting the firm to buy films that were legally available to the public, unaware that it also sold illicit pornographic material.
The suicides have triggered an emotional debate over police tactics and the meaning of justice.
"When magistrates use the press to puff themselves up, I think it neither honours justice nor the press," lawyer Benoit Ducos-Ader said on Sunday.
He announced that he was filing a lawsuit to enable the relatives of Gilbert Pic, 39, to find out "how his name was dragged through the mud".

Pic threw himself from a bridge into the River Garonne in the southwestern city of Bordeaux after being placed under investigation on suspicion of corrupting minors and handling pornographic pictures of minors.

Henri Leclerc, a lawyer and president of the Paris-based League of Human Rights, said the paedophilia probe had become "a witch hunt...based on passion rather than reason" and pleaded for "justice rather than a lynching".
Leclerc told the French daily Liberation that some suspects were totally innocent. "They were detained in the round-up, they were later released, but they are done for," he added.
"Their image has been destroyed for ever," he said.
Leclerc said the crackdown had shed light on paedophilia and thus helped France "confront the truth and finally talk about a hidden phenomenon".

"But there are other consequences: the fears that are created within families, the worried looks that infants give adults and the suspicions that arise about any affectionate relationship with an infant."
